title: Chandi di Var
hook: a Punjabi ballad of the goddess's battle; its first stanza gives the Ardas its opening; Sikhs read its imagery as divine power

segments.voice: Yesterday, Khalsa Mahima: the Guru saying he won, gave and lived by his Sikhs' grace. Your line was by their grace. What did you give back? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-seven.

Stand in a gurdwara at the end of a service. Everyone rises. Hands are folded. One person leads the Ardas, the standing prayer, and its first words are ones Sikhs say at weddings and at funerals, in good times and hard ones: Prithm Bhagauti simar kai. First, remember Bhagauti. Then Guru Nanak. Those words are not from the Guru Granth Sahib. They come from a less expected place: the opening of a war ballad, in Punjabi, by Guru Gobind Singh. Today, that ballad.
screen: `EVERYONE RISES FOR ARDAS.` → `FIRST, REMEMBER BHAGAUTI.` → `FROM A WAR BALLAD.`

segments.voice: Chandi di Var means the ballad of Chandi. A var is a Punjabi ballad, a form for heroes and battles, meant to be sung with drive. Chandi is a name of the goddess known in Hindu stories as Durga, and the ballad tells her battle against demons who had driven the gods from their place. The verses are full of clashing steel, drums and the dust of the field. Then there is the opening stanza. Paraphrased: first remember Bhagauti, then meditate on Guru Nanak, then Angad, Amar Das and Ram Das, then Arjan, Har Gobind and Har Rai, then Har Krishan, whose sight takes away all suffering, then Tegh Bahadur. May they help us everywhere. Those are the lines Sikhs say, standing, at the start of the Ardas, with more added after them. So how do Sikhs read a ballad about a goddess? Sikhs read Bhagauti here as divine power, God's power, and some hear it as the sword, the power that protects the weak. The goddess's battle becomes a picture of that power at work against injustice. As this block began by saying, Sikhs discuss which parts of the Dasam Granth come from the Guru's own pen. Whatever view a Sikh holds, this stanza lives in the Ardas, said standing. What it does is clear: before naming a single Guru, it remembers the power behind them all. Then it lists the Gurus one by one, like a family calling its ancestors by name.
screen: `A VAR: A BALLAD OF BATTLE.` · `CHANDI AGAINST THE DEMONS.` · `FIRST REMEMBER BHAGAUTI, THEN NANAK.` · `READ AS DIVINE POWER.` · then, large: `THE POWER REMEMBERED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read the first stanza. Find it if you can, in Gurmukhi or transliteration or English, and read it slowly, once. Notice the order: power first, then the names. If you can't find it now, use what you heard: first, remember the power; then Nanak; then the Gurus, one by one. Then sit, and let the names go by like a line of people walking past. If you pray, you can rest on the name Waheguru as they pass. The bell holds the time.
Chandi di Var. A Punjabi war ballad by Guru Gobind Singh; its first stanza, first remember Bhagauti, opens the Sikh Ardas. Today's word.
Your line: the power remembered. Today, before one task that scares you a little, pause and remember what holds you up, then start. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Sikhs stand with folded hands for the Ardas at the close of services and before important moments, and its opening lines come from the first stanza of Chandi di Var: first remember Bhagauti, then Guru Nanak and the Gurus after him.
